title: The Global Sour Barrel
dek: The sour grades WCS competes with, Dubai, Mars, Merey: how they are priced, and what moves the arb.

claims.text: Quantum Commodity Intelligence reported on Nov 3 that differentials for the Texas-delivered medium sour crude Southern Green Canyon (SGC), one of the three core grades in the Argus Sour Crude Index alongside Mars and Poseidon, had fallen to a discount of $10 a barrel or greater against West Texas Intermediate (WTI), for a second time this year. The full Quantum report is subscription-only; only its headline and opening line were public in the reporting here.

Discovery Alert reported on the week of Oct 22 to 24, citing OilPrice.com market data, that the Mars premium over West Texas Intermediate (WTI) had fallen to about $6 a barrel, down from $17.50 at the end of March, as US export barrels are held back at home by freight costs. The same report put a US Gulf Coast to Asia VLCC voyage at $60 million to $65 million that week, down from $80 million to $82 million in early October, and cited Valero crude executive Randy Hawkins describing the freight-driven pricing gaps as severe dislocations on the company's Oct 22 earnings call.
claims.vintage: Data: week of Oct 22-24, 2026; published Oct 25, 2026; accessed 2026-11-02
claims.source: Discovery Alert (citing OilPrice.com data and Valero comments)

claims.text: CME public settlement data for the Mars (Argus) vs WTI trade-month spread showed November 2026 settling at a $1.90 per barrel premium on Oct 8, up 18 cents on the day, with October 2026 at $1.75. The positive premium is a partial unwind of the late-September freight-driven softness against WTI, but it remains well off the March crisis premium above $4, per the watch's earlier Argus-cited readings.

Mars crude, the Louisiana medium sour grade, weakened further against West Texas Intermediate (WTI) as rising shipping costs for US-to-Asia routes narrowed the export arb, per Bloomberg reporting on Sep 24. The move makes freight the deciding variable on whether US Gulf sours clear locally or sail to Asia.

Louisiana-delivered Mars settled at $87.65 per barrel in the March 2026 unwind, down about $20 per barrel from the prior session's Argus outright assessment, after comments from US President Donald Trump that the US-Israel war on Iran could end soon triggered a broad selloff. The volume-weighted average premium over West Texas Intermediate (WTI) fell to $4.20 per barrel, about $8.50 per barrel lower than the prior session, with a high-to-low swing of about $10 per barrel. Mars also narrowed from a roughly $13.80 per barrel premium to June Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) Brent futures to about $2.40 per barrel, and Southern Green Canyon traded as low as parity to Domestic Sweet (DSW) crude at Cushing, down from a $7.07 per barrel premium. The snap-back shows how much of the March premium was war risk rather than physical tightness.

Spot trading picked up in the Middle East sour crude market on Oct 14, reflecting healthy demand from end users in Asia, particularly Japan, Hellenic Shipping News reported, citing S&P Global Platts data. The December Brent/Dubai Exchange of Futures for Swaps (EFS) was pegged at $4.04 a barrel at 11 am Singapore time, down 7 cents from the Oct 13 Asian close, but the spread remains wide at firmly above $4, keeping Dubai-linked sour crudes economically favourable for end users. The November-December Dubai crude futures spread was pegged at 98 cents a barrel in backwardation, down 2 cents from the previous Asian close.
claims.source: Hellenic Shipping News (citing S&P Global Platts)

claims.text: S and P Global Platts data showed the November Brent/Dubai Exchange of Futures for Swaps (EFS) at 4.22 dollars a barrel on Sep 27, up 20 cents from the Sep 24 Asian close and its highest since July 8, when it was pegged at 4.29. Traders linked the climb to surging winter gas prices and expectations of gas-to-oil switching demand, while the October/November Dubai timespread held at a 1.03 dollar a barrel backwardation.

The same reporting noted September spot activity from Japan, India and China was minimal, keeping a lid on cash Dubai premiums despite the EFS strength. An unconfirmed Singapore trader report had October-loading Basrah Heavy sold to private Indian refiners at 50 to 70 cents a barrel below its Official Selling Price (OSP), a sign that physical sour premiums are not following paper.

The Brent-Dubai Exchange of Futures for Swaps (EFS), the spread between Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) Brent futures and Dubai swaps, averaged $1.47 per barrel in the first half of January 2026, surged above $6 per barrel by March 3 as the Hormuz freeze took hold, averaged $9.12 per barrel in March, and oscillated between $3.05 and $16.25 per barrel through June and July. In stable conditions the EFS trades around $1.50 to $2.00 per barrel, and past spikes such as Abqaiq in 2019 and the Russia-Ukraine shock in 2022 barely nudged it above $1.50, making the 2026 move unprecedented in both scale and duration. In 2026 the geographic (routing security) component has overwhelmed the quality component, turning the EFS into a proxy for supply security rather than crude type, and it is the key East-West arb signal for Dubai-basket sour grades.

Reuters reported on Nov 5 that spot premiums for Middle East crude benchmarks returned to pre-war levels that week as ample supplies weighed on the market and cooling refining margins in Asia slowed buying interest. Dubai's cash premium to swaps slumped to 65 cents a barrel on Monday, the lowest since July, before recovering to $1.55 a barrel on Thursday, Reuters data showed. Oman's premium dropped to 95 cents a barrel on Tuesday, the weakest since July, before rising to $1.76 on Thursday, against an average of about $8 a barrel in the previous month. Middle East crude flows including bypass pipelines averaged 17.1 million barrels per day in September and 16.3 million in October, Kpler data showed, and Iraqi flows jumped to 3.35 million barrels per day in October, only 150,000 barrels per day under pre-war levels, Kpler analyst Naveen Das said.

Reuters reported on Nov 6 that spot premiums for the Middle East benchmark Dubai fell slightly on Friday, after Saudi Arabia cut its December official selling prices for Asia to a fresh six-year low. The Singapore market had a half trading day on Friday and was closed on Monday for a public holiday, Reuters said via TradingView.

Bloomberg reported on Nov 3 that Middle East oil market metrics pointed to near-term supply outpacing demand for the first time since July: the nearest timespread for the Dubai benchmark was in contango at the start of the week, with the November contract at a discount of about $2 a barrel to December, according to traders and brokers cited by Bloomberg. Partial contracts on the S&P Global Energy trading window, which can be converted into physical barrels and typically command a premium to the Dubai derivatives benchmark, traded at near-parity. Combined exports from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Iraq and Kuwait climbed by 10 percent to just over 15 million barrels per day in October, Bloomberg data showed, while Iranian exports remained effectively halted.

Reuters reported on Nov 2 that spot premiums for Middle East crude benchmarks Oman and Dubai tumbled on Monday to their lowest since mid-July, amid falling oil futures prices and mounting selling pressure, as talks between Iranian and Qatari officials on a deal to end the US-Israeli war on Iran raised hopes of de-escalation. Reuters reported on Nov 4 that the same Oman and Dubai spot premiums edged up on Wednesday, while still hovering around the lowest levels in more than three months due to ample supplies, with a recovery in oil flow via the Strait of Hormuz adding to supplies and refining margins easing.

Reuters reported on Oct 29 that spot premiums for the Middle East crude benchmarks Oman and Dubai ticked lower again, as hopes for revived peace talks weighed on prices: US Vice President JD Vance had sought to restart negotiations with Iran by letter to Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei, the Wall Street Journal reported.

Reuters reported on Oct 27 that spot premiums for Middle East crude benchmarks Oman and Dubai extended their declines, weighed down by ample supplies and weaker buying appetite. Gulf producers and traders cut offer prices to attract demand while buyers held back as crude flows through the Strait of Hormuz increased.

OilPrice.com reported on Oct 21 that the premium of Oman crude over Dubai slumped to $4.22 a barrel, the lowest since the end of July, citing General Index data via Bloomberg. The premium had been as high as $30 a barrel in mid-September and $65 a barrel in March, and eased as Middle East flows recovered on shuttle shipping and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman.

Quantum Commodity Intelligence reported Dubai crude racing higher midweek with Asia distillate cracks rising (its Oct 8 East of Suez note), then easing from its weekly highs on Friday as fears over US military strikes receded. Per QCI's two notes, Dubai premiums are still trading headlines on Middle East security rather than physical spot demand.

Basra Oil Company chief Bassem Abdul Karim said on Sep 24 that the northern leg now carries about 250,000 barrels per day of Basrah crude to Turkey's Mediterranean port of Ceyhan, while southern terminals handled about 2.6 million barrels per day. The same parliamentary hearing put Iraq's war-related revenue loss near 60 billion dollars and flagged sharply higher shipping costs.

Chatham House analysis published Sep 25 describes a proposed revival of the historic Kirkuk-Baniyas corridor, routed via a new hub at Haditha, that would give Baghdad a 2-million-barrel-per-day Hormuz bypass at an estimated cost near 15 billion dollars and roughly four years of construction, reportedly backed by the Trump administration. The piece cautions it diversifies rather than replaces Hormuz, since most Iraqi barrels are bound for China and India, which sit closer to the Gulf than to the Mediterranean.

The Syrian Petroleum Company's Refining Directorate said the first consignment of about 32,800 metric tons of gasoline arrived by tanker at Baniyas and is moving to the Iraqi border by truck under a transit contract with Qatar's UCC Holding, which supplies the fuel and manages transport. Iraq's Oil Ministry confirmed the arrangement; the deal is gasoline-only for now but the route could later carry crude.
claims.vintage: Week of Sep 21-26, 2026; published Sep 26, 2026; accessed 2026-09-28
claims.source: Freedom Bunker (via The Cradle and Reuters)

claims.text: Iraq's crude exports jumped 73 percent in August 2026 to 73 million barrels for the month (about 2.34 million barrels per day), the highest level since the Iran war began, after the State Organization for Marketing of Oil (SOMO) sold Basrah crude at discounts of $25 to $30 per barrel to offset extreme shipping and insurance costs and a small number of Iraqi tankers received special Iranian permission to transit the Strait of Hormuz. The rebound returned more than $4.5 billion of medium-sour crude to the market in a single month, directly relieving the Dubai-basket sour shortfall that had supported Mars and other Atlantic Basin sours.

Iraq's State Organization for Marketing of Oil (SOMO) offered Basrah Medium and Basrah Heavy for collection by ship-to-ship (STS) transfer near the Omani coast for September delivery via tender, the first time since the Iran war began that buyers could lift Iraqi crude outside the Persian Gulf instead of loading deep inside it. Vitol Group and TotalEnergies were among the largest traders moving Iraqi oil during the war, and SOMO also tendered fuel oil for pickup inside or outside the Gulf. If the outside-Hormuz loading point becomes routine, it structurally lowers the freight risk embedded in Basrah pricing and narrows the crisis premium in Dubai-linked grades.

OilPrice.com reported on Oct 19 that global very large crude carrier (VLCC) rates spiked to an all-time high of $805,000 a day in October, about 15 times the recent average, with Rory Johnston cited as putting the cost of shipping crude from the Middle East to China at about $42 a barrel against about $3 normally. The same report said refiners are favouring lighter, sweeter grades that yield more diesel, reducing the appeal of heavy barrels, while renewed Venezuelan flows add competition on the US Gulf Coast.

The US Department of Energy issued a request for proposals on Oct 16 for an exchange of up to 17 million barrels of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR), part of the 172 million barrels Washington agreed to loan under the International Energy Agency's March emergency action, Reuters reported. The take-up precedent is weak: the US had previously offered to loan the last batch from the March deal in June, but companies, required to pay premiums of up to 24 percent in extra barrels returned to the reserve, agreed to borrow only about 500,000 barrels.

Reuters reported on Oct 9 that record tanker freight rates are putting US crude out of reach for Asian refiners, with a very large crude carrier (VLCC) from the Gulf of Mexico to China for November quoted at $80 million this week (Simpson, Spence & Young data on LSEG), closing the US-to-Asia arb. Asian refiners are switching to alternatives from the Middle East and Latin America, and the Murban premium rebounded to over $11 a barrel to Dubai quotes on Thursday, per Reuters. Japanese refiner Cosmo Oil provisionally chartered a VLCC for $81 million to load US oil on Nov 19-21, one of the priciest fixtures on record.

Sparta Commodities' market outlook dated Sep 30 reported that the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) offered 40 million barrels of sour grades under FY26 RFP #4 for delivery in November and December 2026, split 20 million each from Bryan Mound and Big Hill, with bids due Oct 6. The first replacement window for Bryan Mound is Q2 2027 at a 7.5% volumetric interest rate, and Jun-Sep 2027 at 9.5% for Big Hill, versus a minimum 18% on the earlier FY26 Release #2. Sparta's read is that the release should keep US Gulf Coast medium grades under pressure for the balance of the year, and it looks for Mars December FOB to drop below $1 per barrel, revisiting levels last seen in early August. Treat as a trader outlook, not a newsroom report.

The US government's own sour barrel is shifting grade: DOE's August 20 grade table showed the SPR at 101.8 million barrels sweet and 192.3 million sour, and by September 11 the split was 96.8 million sweet and 188.1 million sour (Reuters), meaning sweet drew about 5.0 million barrels against 4.2 million of sour over roughly three weeks. With the reserve at roughly 34% sweet versus DOE's 40% design target, the government's remaining emergency supply is getting more sour-dominant, which limits how much sweet relief a future release could actually deliver to light-sweet markets.
claims.source: US Department of Energy (SPR Quick Facts); Reuters (via Permian Basin Oil and Gas Magazine)

claims.text: US refineries ran at 97 percent utilization in the week ending Sep 11, with no idle capacity left to switch on. US distillate production averaged 5.1 million barrels per day from January through August, the most since 2019, while distillate inventories sat 15.8 million barrels, or 13 percent, below the five-year seasonal average. The read for sour crude: heavy sour barrels with high distillate yields stay bid as long as this lasts.
claims.vintage: Data: week ending Sep 11, 2026; published Sep 21, 2026; accessed 2026-09-28

claims.text: US refinery utilization hit 97.4 percent in late August 2026, the highest since 2018, and shipbroker Gibson reports very little autumn maintenance is confirmed because robust margins keep refiners from taking units offline. The only confirmed turnaround on the Petroleum Administration for Defense District 3 (PADD 3) slate is ExxonMobil's Beaumont fluid catalytic cracking (FCC) unit plus at least two hydrotreaters, running about 45 days from early December to mid-January. PBF pushed Chalmette's crude distillation unit (CDU) and coker into 2027 and CITGO did the same with the Lake Charles coker, while Valero guided third-quarter Gulf Coast throughput at 1.78 to 1.83 million barrels per day. The International Energy Agency (IEA) still expects October North America runs of 18.8 million barrels per day versus 20.5 in August. Sustained near-max runs keep US Gulf Coast (USGC) coker demand for Mars, Western Canadian Select (WCS) and Merey-type barrels elevated, but deferred maintenance raises unplanned-outage risk.

Asian refining margins for 10 parts per million (ppm) sulfur diesel surged to a record just above $87 per barrel in mid-September 2026, versus pre-war levels around $22 per barrel and a prior record of $85.60 set in late March 2026, while the front-month diesel spread stood slightly above $11 per barrel, near a five-month high. Because medium-sour grades carry higher distillate yields than light sweets, record diesel cracks directly support bids for Mars-type barrels and widen the incentive for complex refiners to run heavy sour slates.

Pemex crude exports fell to a 35-year low of about 368,000 barrels per day in December 2025, down 54 percent year over year, as the Olmeca refinery (Dos Bocas) ramped to over 260,000 barrels per day of heavy crude processing and absorbed barrels once destined for export. The export collapse removed roughly 440,000 barrels per day of heavy sour supply year over year, and US imports from Mexico fell to 224,500 barrels per day in December (down 22 percent month over month). With crude production capped at 1.8 million barrels per day under Mexico's Energy Sovereignty 2030 roadmap, the industry may lean more heavily on Western Canadian Select (WCS) or Mars as the Americas heavy benchmark as Maya liquidity dries up.

The Maya export collapse partially reversed as Pemex's refineries stumbled: the Olmeca (Dos Bocas) refinery, with 340,000 barrels per day of nameplate capacity, averaged only 144,000 barrels per day in the second quarter of 2026 (about 42 percent utilization) after a January electrical failure knocked out its coker, catalytic and hydrodesulfurization units, deferring around 150,000 barrels of crude processing. Mexican crude exports averaged about 550,000 barrels per day in March through May 2026, down from roughly 780,000 a year earlier, while fuel imports climbed to 700,000 barrels per day in June. If domestic plants keep underperforming, Maya barrels could swing back onto the US Gulf Coast (USGC) export market, so the heavy-sour shortfall is not one-directional.

BOE Report reported on Nov 9, from Reuters reporting of brokerage assessments, that Western Canadian Select (WCS) for December delivery at Hardisty, Alberta settled at $25 a barrel below West Texas Intermediate (WTI), compared with $26 on Friday, continuing its retreat from the blowout levels of earlier in the month. The discount reached as wide as $31 below WTI in the first week of November, and at Houston WCS barrels in late October hit an all-time wide discount of $23 as soaring global freight rates reduced demand for Canadian crude re-exports off the US Gulf Coast. Global freight rates, while still high, have come down since October, Rory Johnston of Commodity Context told Reuters.

Oil Authority reported, citing Alberta Treasury Board and Finance weekly indicators, that the Western Canadian Select (WCS) discount to West Texas Intermediate (WTI) stood at $30.15 a barrel on Nov 5, holding near its widest level of the fiscal year as crude prices fell, with WTI at $90.52 that day. The differential had reached $30.50 on Oct 29, about 2.1 times the province's $14.80 fiscal-year forecast, Oil Authority calculated from the province's published figures.
claims.source: Oil Authority (citing Alberta Treasury Board and Finance)

claims.text: PrimeXBT reported on Nov 3, citing Investing.com reporting of Modern Commodities and General Index prices, that Western Canadian Select's (WCS) discount in Alberta to a monthly average of West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures expanded to $31.70 a barrel on Tuesday, the widest since November 2018, while Cold Lake crude's discount on the US Gulf Coast reached $23.10, matching levels not seen in eight years. The expanding discount stems from rising global tanker rates and increased imports of competing Venezuelan heavy crude in the US Gulf, and Imperial Oil said on an earnings call the week before that the lower price for Canadian oil was expected to persist through the fourth quarter, PrimeXBT said.
claims.source: PrimeXBT (citing Investing.com, Modern Commodities and General Index)

claims.text: Oil Sands Magazine reported on Oct 29 that the Western Canadian Select (WCS) discount to West Texas Intermediate (WTI) rose from less than $22 a barrel at the end of September to over $31 a barrel, a level last seen above $31 during the pipeline crisis of November 2018. WTI averaged about $97 a barrel in October, and the magazine projected WCS averaging about $70 a barrel for the month, down from $77 in September.

Hart Energy reported on Oct 28 that the Canadian heavy crude discount exceeded $30 a barrel, driven by a supply build-up on the US Gulf Coast from Venezuelan imports and high tanker rates that make exporting oil expensive.

IndexBox reported on Oct 23, citing S and P Global Platts assessments, that Western Canadian Select (WCS) at Hardisty was assessed at a $28.00 a barrel discount to the West Texas Intermediate (WTI) calendar month average on Oct 21, and WCS at Nederland at a $19.50 discount, their lowest levels since November 2023 and December 2022 respectively. Platts sources cited oversupply and increased competition from other heavy crudes entering the US Gulf Coast, such as Venezuela Merey 16.

Venezuela's heavy barrel is finding a new home in Asia: India's imports of Venezuelan crude are set to more than double in October to about 465,000 barrels per day from 196,000 in September, the highest since December 2019, as Reliance Industries' Jamnagar complex takes the cargoes into Sikka, Reuters reported on Oct 8, citing Kpler estimates. Traders put Merey, Venezuela's flagship heavy grade, at a discount of about $16 a barrel to ICE Brent, while freight to India's west coast adds about $33 a barrel; by comparison, Russian Urals is trading at a premium before shipping costs.

Oil Sands Magazine's weekly close for Oct 16 put Western Canadian Select (WCS) at Hardisty at $76.18 a barrel, a $25.00 discount to West Texas Intermediate (WTI), which closed at $101.41. WCS delivered at Houston stood at a $16.60 discount to WTI, WCS at Cushing at $17.92 under, and synthetic crude oil (SCO) at a $7.57 premium to WTI.
